**Capital Airlines** was a United Statestrunk carrier, a scheduled airline serving the eastern, southern, southeastern, and midwestern United States. Capital's headquarters were located at Washington National Airport (now Reagan Washington National Airport) across the Potomac river from Washington, D.C., where crew training and aircraft overhauls were also accomplished.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-2) In the 1950s Capital was the fifth largest United States domestic carrier by passenger count (and sometimes by passenger-miles) after the Big Four air carriers (American, United, TWA, and Eastern).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer,_8_April_1960,_page_516-3)
Capital merged with United Airlines in 1961.

### Clifford Ball Airline
[edit]
Clifford A. Ball, a McKeesport, Pennsylvania, automobile dealer and owner of a controlling interest in Bettis Field near Pittsburgh, won airmail contract route No. 11 on March 27, 1926. In April of the following year, The **Clifford Ball Airline** began operating between Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and Cleveland, Ohio. Clifford Ball Airlines operated from Pittsburgh's first commercial airport, Bettis Field, a former farm field which farmer Barr Peat had allowed to be used for barnstorming.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-4) The airplane which flew the first flight from Pittsburgh to Cleveland, a Waco 9 named "Miss Pittsburgh", is currently displayed at the Pittsburgh International Airport. Famed humorist and performer Will Rogers was known to be an early and regular passenger,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-5) but scheduled passenger service did not begin until April 28, 1928. The following August, Ball Airline became the first airline to serve Washington, D.C., from the west, offering its flagship "Path of the Eagle" service from Cleveland to Hoover Field across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-6) A "Path of the Eagle" brochure and schedule are displayed at the Pitcairn Field Web site.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-PitcairnField-7)

### Pennsylvania Air Lines
[edit]
Ball sold his interests in November 1930 to Pittsburgh Aviation Industries Corp., and the airline became **Pennsylvania Air Lines** (PAL). PAL was reorganized as **Pennsylvania Airlines** after the Air Mail scandal of the early 1930s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-8) In 1934 Pennsylvania Airlines acquired **Kohler Aviation**.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_10-9)
Not to be confused with Central Airlines, the Texas-based regional airline.
**Central Airlines** was founded in 1934 by the men who had formed **Pittsburgh Airlines** in 1929.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-10) Central was notable for hiring Helen Richey, the first female commercial pilot in the U.S.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-11) Central Airlines became PAL's main competitor and they engaged in ruinous rate wars with prices well below those charged for railroad seats.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-13)
The two companies merged to form **Pennsylvania Central Airlines**, or **PCA**, on November 1, 1936.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_23-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-15)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
[edit]
DC-3 of Pennsylvania Central Airlines
The merged airlines flew Stinson A and Boeing 247 aircraft.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-16) Early in its existence, PCA faced a minor crisis in January 1937 when the Bureau of Air Commerce temporarily grounded the airline's Boeing 247s.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-17) The six B-247s were all sold off in 1937. The airline's 15 B-247Ds were all gone by the end of 1942. Two remain in museums today—one at the National Aviation Museum at Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, and another, the _City of Renton_, in flying condition at the Museum of Flight, Boeing Field, Seattle, Washington.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-18)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
PCA, based at the new Allegheny County Airport near Pittsburgh, continued to add routes, notably to Chicago in 1938, and aircraft, notably the Douglas DC-3, in 1940.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-19) In 1941 PCA moved its headquarters to the new Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, becoming one of its three original tenants; PCA had been consulted during the airport's design. The row of office buildings next to its hangars became "mahogany row" and the airline adopted the slogan "The Capital Airline", with its aircraft dubbed "Capitaliners".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-20) In September 1943 Pennsylvania Central requested the CAB authorize new routes affecting 23 states indicating plans for a major expansion after the war.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-21) PCA even had big trans-Atlantic ambitions.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-23) PCA did see expansion as the war wound down.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-25) The company signed contracts with Douglas Aircraft for DC-4s, on September 28, 1944, worth $10 million.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-26)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
In 1946 PCA began flying the Douglas DC-4 but found the airplane was unprofitable on some of its low volume short segment routes. One of PCA's DC-4s had been used to transport President Roosevelt to the Casablanca Conference during World War II[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-27) Ten DC-4s still served Capital at the time of the UAL merger. All were immediately disposed of by United.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_10-9)
By 1946, the combination of expansion and post-war inflation were financially pressing United States airlines.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-29) PCA was facing stronger competition on the essential New York to Chicago route.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-30) By the end of the first quarter of 1947 Pennsylvania-Central was in such a bad situation that the company president had to seek S.E.C. approval for a refinancing agreement with PCA's bankers.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-31)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
The crisis led PCA to the election of J.H. "Slim" Charmichael as president, and drastic cuts from 4,800 employees to 3,000.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-32) By October 1, 1947, PCA had 25 DC-3s (two cargo only) and three DC-4s. "We had a sick airline on our hands, and we had to get it out of bed, but quickly. We figured our best chance lay in leading not just following the others", Charmichael told the New York Times.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-33) The cuts were followed by the acquisition of used, but newer, equipment and the situation was saved.
By 1947 PCA's route network no longer reflected its name. On April 21, 1948, the airline adopted a new insignia, colors and the name **Capital Airlines**.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_12-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-35)
In 1948 Capital introduced the "Nighthawk", one of the first coach class services, to compete with the railroads between Chicago and New York City, as well as the dominant airlines on the route, United, TWA and American.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer,_8_April_1960,_page_516-3) Each flight left at 1 AM and stopped for ten minutes at Pittsburgh (Allegheny County). Chicago-NY fare was $29.60 plus 15% federal tax; seats on all other flights cost $44.10 plus tax.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_12-34)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
Also in 1948 the first airborne television was installed on a Capital airplane.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-36)
A Capital Airlines Vickers Viscount at Allentown, Pennsylvania, discharging passengers in 1960.
In 1950 Capital Airlines received its first Lockheed Constellations. In 1955 Capital became the first U.S. operator of the British manufactured, four engine Vickers Viscount, the first passenger turboprop airliner.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer,_October_14,_1955,_page_631-37) The Viscount propjets were deployed on the flagship Washington-Chicago route and the airline had planned to fly them on expanded service; however, Capital was mostly stymied by the federal Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer,_March_15,_1957,_page_351-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer_January_31,_1958,_page_157-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer_February_14,_1958,_page_222-40) The CAB also refused Capital a requested subsidy.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-41) Still, Capital's passenger-miles in 1957 were 88% more than 1955._[citation needed_]

### Acquisition by and merger with United
was the largest airline merger in history at that time.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Lemmon,_Captain_R_2015,_page_155-53) Despite a year of planning, all did not go smoothly on merger day.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-54) United continued to operate forty-one of Capital's Viscount propjets as well as three of Capital's Douglas DC-3s.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Lemmon,_Captain_R_2015,_page_155-53) United soon purchased six Viscounts which Capital had returned to Vickers.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-55) United operated three ex-PCA/Capital DC-3s for one year after the merger.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-56) United had retired its last DC-3s in the 1950s. Because of the need to operate CAB route award AM-34, it suddenly became the last major United States airline to operate the DC-3.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-57)

### The New Capital Airlines
[edit]
In 1981, former employees formed the Capital Airlines Association to preserve their memories of the old carrier. A retired United Airlines pilot, Milt Marshall, bought the Capital trademark and operated a charter business under the Capital name out of Waterbury-Oxford Airport in Connecticut.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-58)
In a bizarre final chapter to the brand's story, in July 2004 Capt. Marshall was transporting a passenger in a Capital Airways Piper PA-31 Navajo from Waterbury to upstate New York. The plane crashed as it made an approach in clear weather near Lake George. Both pilot and passenger were killed. Their bodies were mangled and burned in the wreckage. A pistol magazine with two missing rounds was found at the crash scene, but no gun was ever found. Many people believe that the passenger, a businessman who was facing both bankruptcy and indictment for fraud, and who had attempted to buy a large life insurance policy just prior to the flight, killed the pilot and himself, causing the crash. The bodies were so mutilated that no official cause of death was determined and the case was closed. This marked the last chapter of Capital Airlines.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-60)

## Destinations: 1937–1960
[edit]
In 1937, PCA's main route was from Milwaukee to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), with stops in Muskegon, Grand Rapids, Lansing, Detroit, Cleveland, Akron, and Pittsburgh. Spurs ran from Detroit to Pontiac and Flint, and from Pittsburgh to Parkersburg and Charleston.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-61)
By 1941, new spurs were added from Grand Rapids to Chicago, Sault Ste. Marie and Traverse City; from Pittsburgh to Erie and Buffalo; and from Charleston to Tri-Cities, Knoxville, Chattanooga, and Birmingham. New routes ran north from Washington to Baltimore, Harrisburg and Williamsport, and south to Norfolk, then across North Carolina serving Rocky Mount, Raleigh, Greensboro, Hickory, and Asheville.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-62) Pittsburgh-New York City service was added by 1946.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-63)
By 1950 the network extended south to Atlanta, Mobile, and New Orleans, and west to Minneapolis.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-64)Memphis and Huntsville were added by 1953, along with interchange service on National Airlines to Florida.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-65)
By 1960, the year before its merger with United, Capital served Florida with its own aircraft on flights to Jacksonville, Miami, St. Petersburg, Tampa, and West Palm Beach.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-66)

1946
Delta officially enters cargo business. One-millionth passenger boards. Delta is first airline to fly nonstop Chicago-Miami, initially withDouglas DC-4 planes.
1947
Delta's fleet totals 644 available seats. Receives National Safety Award for more than one-half billion passenger miles without a fatality. Scheduled all-cargo flights begin. Delta Vacations program begins as Millionaire Dream Vacations (later Delta Dream Vacations) with packaged summer vacations to Miami.
1948
Begins interchange service with TWA personnel flying Delta planes from Cincinnati to Detroit and Delta crews flying TWA ships south from Cincinnati to Atlanta, Miami and Dallas. The Douglas DC-6 is the first Delta plane with cabin pressurization, air conditioning, seat tray tables for meals and a 6-seat Sky Lounge.
1949
Coach Class service starts; discounted-fare "Owly Bird" night flights between Chicago and Miami.
Through the Decades: 1950's
Delta expands internationally, pioneers extensive hub-and-spoke operations
1950
First official Delta souvenir for children, a paper Junior Pilot Certificate—handed out to both girls and boys.
1952
Delta flies Convair 340 planes; modified to Model-440 standards in 1956
1953
Chicago and Southern Air Lines merger brings Delta its first international routes to the Caribbean and Caracas. Airline called Delta-C&S for the next two years. Delta inherits from C&S its first customer recognition program—Flying Colonel, one of air transport’s coveted awards. Lockheed Constellations join the fleet.
1954
First class service begins, as Golden Crown Service on Douglas DC-7 flights. Delta introduces reserved seats—Golden Crown customers can select their seat when they check in at the airport. First airline to supplement visual inspection of aircraft parts with a portable x-ray machine to examine interior structures..
1957
Delta airport lounges (today's Sky Clubs) introduced when Delta opens a Golden Crown Room at the Atlanta airport with invitation-only access for VIP guests. In 1958/59, the name was shortened to "Crown Room." By 1961, Delta had Crown Rooms at Atlanta, Miami, Dallas and Detroit.

Forklifts and conveyer belts installed for handling cargo and baggage in all larger cities served by Delta. A new truck lift cuts in half the time it takes to load and unload planes.
1958
LuxuriousDouglas DC-7Royal Service first-class flights offer three—instead of the usual two—flight attendants, boarding music by Muzak, complimentary champagne and steaks cooked to order. Children receive Delta’s first “kiddie wings” souvenir pins.
1959
Delta is first airline to launch Douglas DC-8 jet service. The red, white, and blue triangle "widget" becomes Delta's logo, resembling the swept-wing appearance of a jet. First airline to offer complimentary meals on discounted coach flights.
1959
First baby born on a Delta flight: Suzanne Ector, over Malden, Missouri, at 9,000 feet. Flight attendant wings are used as diaper pins.

PAL was reorganized as **Pennsylvania Airlines** after the Air Mail scandal of the early 1930s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-8) In 1934 Pennsylvania Airlines acquired **Kohler Aviation**.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_10-9)
Not to be confused with Central Airlines, the Texas-based regional airline.
**Central Airlines** was founded in 1934 by the men who had formed **Pittsburgh Airlines** in 1929.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-10) Central was notable for hiring Helen Richey, the first female commercial pilot in the U.S.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-11) Central Airlines became PAL's main competitor and they engaged in ruinous rate wars with prices well below those charged for railroad seats.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-13)
The two companies merged to form **Pennsylvania Central Airlines**, or **PCA**, on November 1, 1936.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_23-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-15)

The merged airlines flew Stinson A and Boeing 247 aircraft.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-16) Early in its existence, PCA faced a minor crisis in January 1937 when the Bureau of Air Commerce temporarily grounded the airline's Boeing 247s.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-17) The six B-247s were all sold off in 1937. The airline's 15 B-247Ds were all gone by the end of 1942. Two remain in museums today—one at the National Aviation Museum at Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, and another, the _City of Renton_, in flying condition at the Museum of Flight, Boeing Field, Seattle, Washington.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-18)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
PCA, based at the new Allegheny County Airport near Pittsburgh, continued to add routes, notably to Chicago in 1938, and aircraft, notably the Douglas DC-3, in 1940.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-19) In 1941 PCA moved its headquarters to the new Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, becoming one of its three original tenants; PCA had been consulted during the airport's design. The row of office buildings next to its hangars became "mahogany row" and the airline adopted the slogan "The Capital Airline", with its aircraft dubbed "Capitaliners".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-20) In September 1943 Pennsylvania Central requested the CAB authorize new routes affecting 23 states indicating plans for a major expansion after the war.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-21) PCA even had big trans-Atlantic ambitions.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-23) PCA did see expansion as the war wound down.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-25) The company signed contracts with Douglas Aircraft for DC-4s, on September 28, 1944, worth $10 million.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-26)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
In 1946 PCA began flying the Douglas DC-4 but found the airplane was unprofitable on some of its low volume short segment routes. One of PCA's DC-4s had been used to transport President Roosevelt to the Casablanca Conference during World War II[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-27) Ten DC-4s still served Capital at the time of the UAL merger. All were immediately disposed of by United.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_10-9)
By 1946, the combination of expansion and post-war inflation were financially pressing United States airlines.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-29) PCA was facing stronger competition on the essential New York to Chicago route.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-30) By the end of the first quarter of 1947 Pennsylvania-Central was in such a bad situation that the company president had to seek S.E.C. approval for a refinancing agreement with PCA's bankers.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-31)

### Pennsylvania Central Airlines
The crisis led PCA to the election of J.H. "Slim" Charmichael as president, and drastic cuts from 4,800 employees to 3,000.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-32) By October 1, 1947, PCA had 25 DC-3s (two cargo only) and three DC-4s. "We had a sick airline on our hands, and we had to get it out of bed, but quickly. We figured our best chance lay in leading not just following the others", Charmichael told the New York Times.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-33) The cuts were followed by the acquisition of used, but newer, equipment and the situation was saved.
By 1947 PCA's route network no longer reflected its name. On April 21, 1948, the airline adopted a new insignia, colors and the name **Capital Airlines**.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_12-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-35)
In 1948 Capital introduced the "Nighthawk", one of the first coach class services, to compete with the railroads between Chicago and New York City, as well as the dominant airlines on the route, United, TWA and American.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Flight_&_Aircraft_Engineer,_8_April_1960,_page_516-3) Each flight left at 1 AM and stopped for ten minutes at Pittsburgh (Allegheny County). Chicago-NY fare was $29.60 plus 15% federal tax; seats on all other flights cost $44.10 plus tax.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-Bohl,_Walt_2001,_page_12-34)

texts.12:
### The New Capital Airlines
[edit]
In 1981, former employees formed the Capital Airlines Association to preserve their memories of the old carrier. A retired United Airlines pilot, Milt Marshall, bought the Capital trademark and operated a charter business under the Capital name out of Waterbury-Oxford Airport in Connecticut.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-58)
In a bizarre final chapter to the brand's story, in July 2004 Capt. Marshall was transporting a passenger in a Capital Airways Piper PA-31 Navajo from Waterbury to upstate New York. The plane crashed as it made an approach in clear weather near Lake George. Both pilot and passenger were killed. Their bodies were mangled and burned in the wreckage. A pistol magazine with two missing rounds was found at the crash scene, but no gun was ever found. Many people believe that the passenger, a businessman who was facing both bankruptcy and indictment for fraud, and who had attempted to buy a large life insurance policy just prior to the flight, killed the pilot and himself, causing the crash. The bodies were so mutilated that no official cause of death was determined and the case was closed. This marked the last chapter of Capital Airlines.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Airlines_(United_States)#cite_note-60)

A **day** is the timeperiod of a full [rotation of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_rotation "Earth's rotation") with respect to the Sun. On average, this is 24 hours (86,400 seconds). As a day passes at a given location it experiences morning, afternoon, evening, and night. This daily cycle drives circadian rhythms in many organisms, which are vital to many life processes.
A collection of sequential days is organized into calendars as dates, almost always into weeks, months, and years. A solar calendar organizes dates based on the Sun's annual cycle, giving consistent start dates for the four seasons from year to year. A lunar calendar organizes dates based on the Moon's lunar phase.
In common usage, a day starts at midnight, written as 00:00 or 12:00 am in 24- or 12-hour clocks, respectively. Because the time of midnight varies between locations, time zones are set up to facilitate the use of a uniform standard time. Other conventions exist for marking the beginning and end of days, such as the Jewish religious calendar which counts days beginning at sunset, or in astronomy, in which a day begins at noon so that observations throughout a single night are recorded as happening on the same day.
In specific applications, the definition of a day is slightly modified, such as in the SI day (exactly 86,400 seconds) used for computers and standards keeping, local mean time accounting of the Earth's natural fluctuation of a solar day, and stellar day and sidereal day (using the celestial sphere) used for astronomy. In some countries outside of the tropics, daylight saving time is practiced, and each year there will be one 23-hour civil day and one 25-hour civil day. Due to slight variations in the rotation of the Earth, there are rare times when a leap second will get inserted at the end of a UTC day, and so while almost all days have a duration of 86,400 seconds, there are these exceptional cases of a day with 86,401 seconds (in the half-century spanning 1972 through 2022, there have been a total of 27 leap seconds that have been inserted, so roughly once every other year).

The term comes from the Old English term _dæġ_ (/dæj/), with its cognates such as _dagur_ in Icelandic, _Tag_ in German, and _dag_ in Norwegian, Danish, Swedish and Dutch – all stemming from a Proto-Germanic root _*dagaz_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:0-1)

### Apparent and mean solar day
[edit]
Earth's rotation imaged by Deep Space Climate Observatory, showing axis tilt
Several definitions of this universal human concept are used according to context, need, and convenience. Besides the day of 24 hours (86,400 seconds), the word _day_ is used for several different spans of time based on the rotation of the Earth around its axis. An important one is the _solar day_, the time it takes for the Sun to return to its culmination point (its highest point in the sky). Due to an orbit's eccentricity, the Sun resides in one of the orbit's foci instead of the middle. Consequently, due to [Kepler's second law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler's_laws_of_planetary_motion#Second_law "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"), the planet travels at different speeds at various positions in its orbit, and thus a solar day is not the same length of time throughout the orbital year. Because the Earth moves along an eccentric orbit around the Sun while the Earth spins on an inclined axis, this period can be up to 7.9 seconds more than (or less than) 24 hours. In recent decades, the average length of a solar day on Earth has been about 86,400.002 seconds[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-2) (24.000 000 6 hours). There are currently about 365.2421875 solar days in one mean tropical year.
Ancient custom has a new day starting at either the rising or setting of the Sun on the local horizon (Italian reckoning, for example, being 24 hours from sunset, old style).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-3) The exact moment of, and the interval between, two sunrises or sunsets depends on the geographical position (longitude and latitude, as well as altitude), and the time of year (as indicated by ancient hemispherical sundials).

### Apparent and mean solar day
A more constant day can be defined by the Sun passing through the local meridian, which happens at local noon (upper culmination) or midnight (lower culmination). The exact moment is dependent on the geographical longitude, and to a lesser extent on the time of the year. The length of such a day is nearly constant (24 hours ± 30 seconds). This is the time as indicated by modern sundials.
A further improvement defines a fictitious mean Sun that moves with constant speed along the celestial equator; the speed is the same as the average speed of the real Sun, but this removes the variation over a year as the Earth moves along its orbit around the Sun (due to both its velocity and its axial tilt).
In terms of Earth's rotation, the average day length is about 360.9856°. A day lasts for more than 360° of rotation because of the Earth's revolution around the Sun. With a full year being slightly more than 360 days, the Earth's daily orbit around the Sun is slightly less than 1°, so the day is slightly less than 361° of rotation.
Elsewhere in the Solar System or other parts of the universe, a day is a full rotation of other large astronomical objects with respect to its star.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-4)
For civil purposes, a common clock time is typically defined for an entire region based on the local mean solar time at a central meridian. Such _time zones_ began to be adopted about the middle of the 19th century when railroads with regularly occurring schedules came into use, with most major countries having adopted them by 1929. As of 2015, throughout the world, 40 such zones are now in use: the central zone, from which all others are defined as offsets, is known as UTC+00, which uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
The most common convention starts the civil day at midnight: this is near the time of the lower culmination of the Sun on the central meridian of the time zone. Such a day may be called a calendar day.
A day is commonly divided into 24 hours, with each hour being made up of 60 minutes, and each minute composed of 60 seconds.
Rotation of the dwarf planet Ceres

### Apparent and mean solar day
A sidereal day or stellar day is the span of time it takes for the Earth to make one entire rotation[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-5) with respect to the celestial background or a distant star (assumed to be fixed).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:1-6) Measuring a day as such is used in astronomy.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:1-6) A sidereal day is about 4 minutes less than a solar day of 24 hours (23 hours 56 minutes and 4.09 seconds), or 0.99726968 of a solar day of 24 hours.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-Allen296-7) There are about 366.2422 stellar days in one mean tropical year (one stellar day more than the number of solar days).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-8)
Besides a stellar day on Earth, other bodies in the Solar System have day times, the durations of these being:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-VRG-20190118-10)
| Name | Daylength (hours) |  
| --- | --- |  
| Mercury | 4 222.6 |  
| Venus | 2802 |  
| Earth's Moon | 708.7 |  
| Mars | 24.7 |  
| Ceres | 9[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-11)–9.1[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-12) |  
| Jupiter | 9.9 |

### In the International System of Units
[edit]
The day is not a unit in the International System of Units (SI), though prior to 2026 it was described as accepted for use with SI.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-Non-SI-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-14) A day, with symbol d, is defined using SI units as 86,400 seconds; the second is the base unit of time in SI units.

### In decimal and metric time
[edit]
Decimal clock face, made in around the start of the 19th century
Various decimal or metric time proposals have been made, but do not redefine the day, and use the day or sidereal day as a base unit. Metric time uses metric prefixes to keep time. It uses the day as the base unit, and smaller units being fractions of a day: a metric hour (_deci_) is 1⁄10 of a day; a metric minute (_milli_) is 1⁄1000 of a day; etc.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-15) Similarly, in decimal time, the length of a day is static to normal time. A day is also split into 10 hours, and 10 days comprise a _décade –_ the equivalent of a week. 3 _décades_ make a month.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):35 Various decimal time proposals which do not redefine the day: Henri de Sarrauton's proposal kept days, and subdivided hours into 100 minutes;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):42 in Mendizábal y Tamborel's proposal, the sidereal day was the basic unit, with subdivisions made upon it;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):42–43 and Rey-Pailhade's proposal divided the day 100 _cés.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite\_note-:5-16):42_
The word refers to various similarly defined ideas, such as:
Full day

### In decimal and metric time
*   A full dark and light period, sometimes called a _nychthemeron_ in English, from the Greek for _night-day_,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-17) or more colloquially the term _24 hours_. Other languages may also have a separate word for a full day.  
*   A day counting approximation, for example "See you in three days." or "the following day"  
*   Part of a date: the day of the year (_doy_) in ordinal dates, day of the month (_dom_) in calendar dates or day of the week (_dow_) in week dates.  
*   Time regularly spend at paid work on a single work day, cf. man-day and workweek.
Daytime
*   The period of light when the Sun is above the local horizon (that is, the time period from sunrise to sunset)  
*   The time period from first-light "dawn" to last-light "dusk".
Other
*   A specific period of the day, which may vary by context, such as "the school day" or "the work day".

A **day** is the timeperiod of a full [rotation of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_rotation "Earth's rotation") with respect to the Sun. On average, this is 24 hours (86,400 seconds). As a day passes at a given location it experiences morning, afternoon, evening, and night. This daily cycle drives circadian rhythms in many organisms, which are vital to many life processes.
A collection of sequential days is organized into calendars as dates, almost always into weeks, months, and years. A solar calendar organizes dates based on the Sun's annual cycle, giving consistent start dates for the four seasons from year to year. A lunar calendar organizes dates based on the Moon's lunar phase.
In common usage, a day starts at midnight, written as 00:00 or 12:00 am in 24- or 12-hour clocks, respectively. Because the time of midnight varies between locations, time zones are set up to facilitate the use of a uniform standard time. Other conventions exist for marking the beginning and end of days, such as the Jewish religious calendar which counts days beginning at sunset, or in astronomy, in which a day begins at noon so that observations throughout a single night are recorded as happening on the same day.
In specific applications, the definition of a day is slightly modified, such as in the SI day (exactly 86,400 seconds) used for computers and standards keeping, local mean time accounting of the Earth's natural fluctuation of a solar day, and stellar day and sidereal day (using the celestial sphere) used for astronomy. In some countries outside of the tropics, daylight saving time is practiced, and each year there will be one 23-hour civil day and one 25-hour civil day. Due to slight variations in the rotation of the Earth, there are rare times when a leap second will get inserted at the end of a UTC day, and so while almost all days have a duration of 86,400 seconds, there are these exceptional cases of a day with 86,401 seconds (in the half-century spanning 1972 through 2022, there have been a total of 27 leap seconds that have been inserted, so roughly once every other year).
texts.1: The term comes from the Old English term _dæġ_ (/dæj/), with its cognates such as _dagur_ in Icelandic, _Tag_ in German, and _dag_ in Norwegian, Danish, Swedish and Dutch – all stemming from a Proto-Germanic root _*dagaz_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:0-1)
texts.2:
### Apparent and mean solar day
[edit]
Earth's rotation imaged by Deep Space Climate Observatory, showing axis tilt
Several definitions of this universal human concept are used according to context, need, and convenience. Besides the day of 24 hours (86,400 seconds), the word _day_ is used for several different spans of time based on the rotation of the Earth around its axis. An important one is the _solar day_, the time it takes for the Sun to return to its culmination point (its highest point in the sky). Due to an orbit's eccentricity, the Sun resides in one of the orbit's foci instead of the middle. Consequently, due to [Kepler's second law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler's_laws_of_planetary_motion#Second_law "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"), the planet travels at different speeds at various positions in its orbit, and thus a solar day is not the same length of time throughout the orbital year. Because the Earth moves along an eccentric orbit around the Sun while the Earth spins on an inclined axis, this period can be up to 7.9 seconds more than (or less than) 24 hours. In recent decades, the average length of a solar day on Earth has been about 86,400.002 seconds[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-2) (24.000 000 6 hours). There are currently about 365.2421875 solar days in one mean tropical year.
Ancient custom has a new day starting at either the rising or setting of the Sun on the local horizon (Italian reckoning, for example, being 24 hours from sunset, old style).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-3) The exact moment of, and the interval between, two sunrises or sunsets depends on the geographical position (longitude and latitude, as well as altitude), and the time of year (as indicated by ancient hemispherical sundials).
texts.3:
### Apparent and mean solar day
A more constant day can be defined by the Sun passing through the local meridian, which happens at local noon (upper culmination) or midnight (lower culmination). The exact moment is dependent on the geographical longitude, and to a lesser extent on the time of the year. The length of such a day is nearly constant (24 hours ± 30 seconds). This is the time as indicated by modern sundials.
A further improvement defines a fictitious mean Sun that moves with constant speed along the celestial equator; the speed is the same as the average speed of the real Sun, but this removes the variation over a year as the Earth moves along its orbit around the Sun (due to both its velocity and its axial tilt).
In terms of Earth's rotation, the average day length is about 360.9856°. A day lasts for more than 360° of rotation because of the Earth's revolution around the Sun. With a full year being slightly more than 360 days, the Earth's daily orbit around the Sun is slightly less than 1°, so the day is slightly less than 361° of rotation.
Elsewhere in the Solar System or other parts of the universe, a day is a full rotation of other large astronomical objects with respect to its star.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-4)
For civil purposes, a common clock time is typically defined for an entire region based on the local mean solar time at a central meridian. Such _time zones_ began to be adopted about the middle of the 19th century when railroads with regularly occurring schedules came into use, with most major countries having adopted them by 1929. As of 2015, throughout the world, 40 such zones are now in use: the central zone, from which all others are defined as offsets, is known as UTC+00, which uses Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
The most common convention starts the civil day at midnight: this is near the time of the lower culmination of the Sun on the central meridian of the time zone. Such a day may be called a calendar day.
A day is commonly divided into 24 hours, with each hour being made up of 60 minutes, and each minute composed of 60 seconds.

### Apparent and mean solar day
A sidereal day or stellar day is the span of time it takes for the Earth to make one entire rotation[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-5) with respect to the celestial background or a distant star (assumed to be fixed).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:1-6) Measuring a day as such is used in astronomy.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:1-6) A sidereal day is about 4 minutes less than a solar day of 24 hours (23 hours 56 minutes and 4.09 seconds), or 0.99726968 of a solar day of 24 hours.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-Allen296-7) There are about 366.2422 stellar days in one mean tropical year (one stellar day more than the number of solar days).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-8)
Besides a stellar day on Earth, other bodies in the Solar System have day times, the durations of these being:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-VRG-20190118-10)

| Venus | 2802 |  
| Earth's Moon | 708.7 |  
| Mars | 24.7 |  
| Ceres | 9[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-11)–9.1[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-12) |  
| Jupiter | 9.9 |  
| Saturn | 10.7 |  
| Uranus | 17.2 |

### In the International System of Units
[edit]
The day is not a unit in the International System of Units (SI), though prior to 2026 it was described as accepted for use with SI.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-Non-SI-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-14) A day, with symbol d, is defined using SI units as 86,400 seconds; the second is the base unit of time in SI units.
texts.6:
### In decimal and metric time
[edit]
Decimal clock face, made in around the start of the 19th century
Various decimal or metric time proposals have been made, but do not redefine the day, and use the day or sidereal day as a base unit. Metric time uses metric prefixes to keep time. It uses the day as the base unit, and smaller units being fractions of a day: a metric hour (_deci_) is 1⁄10 of a day; a metric minute (_milli_) is 1⁄1000 of a day; etc.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-15) Similarly, in decimal time, the length of a day is static to normal time. A day is also split into 10 hours, and 10 days comprise a _décade –_ the equivalent of a week. 3 _décades_ make a month.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):35 Various decimal time proposals which do not redefine the day: Henri de Sarrauton's proposal kept days, and subdivided hours into 100 minutes;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):42 in Mendizábal y Tamborel's proposal, the sidereal day was the basic unit, with subdivisions made upon it;[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-:5-16):42–43 and Rey-Pailhade's proposal divided the day 100 _cés.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite\_note-:5-16):42_
The word refers to various similarly defined ideas, such as:

*   A full dark and light period, sometimes called a _nychthemeron_ in English, from the Greek for _night-day_,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day#cite_note-17) or more colloquially the term _24 hours_. Other languages may also have a separate word for a full day.  
*   A day counting approximation, for example "See you in three days." or "the following day"

Celestine Karoney BBC Africa Sport, Nairobi
AFP
**Athletes often have that one thing that fuels their determination to succeed and for women's marathon world record-holder Brigid Kosgei, it is her difficult childhood.**
"When I think back to my humble beginnings and the challenges we went through growing up, I tell myself I cannot go back to that life and it pushes me to do well," the 25-year-old Kenyan athlete told the BBC.
Four years since running her first marathon, which she won, Kosgei is now the fastest woman in history over the 26.2-mile (42.2km) distance.
Last week in the US city of Chicago, she smashed the record set by Briton Paula Radcliffe in London 16 years ago, by a staggering 81 seconds.
Her two hours 14 minutes and four seconds record was six months in the making - with her coach, Eric Kimaiyo, quietly planning the assault.
In September, Kosgei opted not to honour an invitation to represent her country at the World Athletics Championships in Doha.
"We asked for her to be excused because we had planned something special but we didn't speak about it because we didn't want to put her under any pressure," Kimaiyo told the BBC.
But her discipline and dedication is something that has always set her apart.
"You could tell she was a very talented athlete even in training, extremely disciplined and competitive, never liked to be outshone in training," Robert Ngisirei, who coached her while in high school, told the BBC.

# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## Jogging to school
She was one of seven children raised by a single mother in Elgeyo-Marakwet county, a region in the Rift Valley known to produce some of Kenya's top runners.
And like some other Kenyan athletes before her, Kosgei discovered she could run while in primary school, when she had to jog to class in the morning.
"My school was 10km from home and sometimes to avoid getting late I would run. On my way I met athletes who were training and said to myself: 'I can be like them,'" she said.
London 2012: The village at the heart of Kenyan long-distance running
She started competing in middle-distance events at school and though she was never selected to represent her country, her talent was never in doubt.
After raising school fees became a challenge for her mother, Kosgei decided to drop out of school in January 2012 during her final year, given that her studies were now coming second to her track training.
"By the time I was in form three, the arrears were over $1,500 (£1,200). My mother tried to convince me to stay on by saying she would borrow the money but I told her: 'For how long will we keep borrowing?"

# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## Career break to have twins
But now, aged 17, she was able to take her running seriously - something that has repaid her family in spades and pays for all her younger siblings' school fees.
She began training with her boyfriend Mathew Kosgei, who is now her husband. A year later she took a career break after giving birth to twins.
But motherhood did not dent her determination. In 2015 she picked up where she had left off, this time moving to join a training camp not far from her home, run by her coach.
**You may also be interested in:**
*   Born to run: Kenya's top runners  
*   Technology behind record marathon runs
Such camps in Kenya offer athletes an environment where they can focus on training away from the distractions of everyday life.
For female athletes, the decision to stay away from their families, especially children, is often a difficult one but those who do it usually have good family support.
"My husband told me not to worry - he would take care of the children - and that I should just focus on my career and soon the children also got used to seeing me only on the weekends when I'd return home," said Kosgei.

# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## 'My mother is very happy'
Within months of joining the camp, she ran her first marathon, in November 2015 in Portugal, romping home in first place, beating the competition by more than four minutes.
Her decision to go into marathon running was informed by the very competitive nature of track events.
At her training camp there were more marathon runners and it was easier for her to get training partners.
She now trains with her male teammates to improve her endurance.
"It is very difficult training with them because they are very fast but when I want to give up, I tell myself: 'No, keep moving.'"
Her season is over but she is ranked the top female marathon runner of 2019. Next year her focus will turn to the biggest sports event of all - the Olympic Games.
She is now heading back to her home village to visit her mum, for whom she has bought land and a house with her previous winnings, and will spend time with her husband and children.
"My mother is waiting for me to get back home and she was very happy when I broke the record," she said.

Whiting: Pregnant at 15, she's now a professor

Source: https://www.ocregister.com/2012/11/30/whiting-pregnant-at-15-shes-now-a-professor/
Title: Whiting: Pregnant at 15, she’s now a professor
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Sometimes a mistake turns into the best decision you ever made.
I meet Thea Gavin, grandmother of five, and can’t help staring at her feet.
Yes, feet.
Gavin, professor at Concordia University Irvine and recipient of two master’s degrees, isn’t wearing shoes. Or socks.
Since Gavin’s a barefoot runner, her lack of footwear is expected. We head off on a run, with me wearing shoes. As we run and chat, Gavin’s life story starts to unfold, and I realize her story is about far more than running barefoot.
It’s about trust, love and faith.
It’s also about a high school dropout who had her first child at 16.
Yes, _those_ were mistakes.
But her recent rim-to-rim Grand Canyon hike – barefoot – was intentional.
• • •
Ever the professor, Gavin agrees to share if I promise to make this column a teachable moment – and funny.
Funny’s hard and the professor’s assignment scares the bejeebers out of me. But what scares me more is knowing that at some time during our run, according to my own weird code, I must remove my shoes and run barefoot.
Why run shoeless? I call it reporting. My wife calls it nuts.
Gavin, 53, glides along a rocky trail as if she were born to run.
For a few hundred yards, I run on soft dirt and feel like Huck Finn. Then I hit a rough patch. Ouch. Then pebbles. Ouch, ouch. Then rocks…
I blurt something one shouldn’t, especially around a Christian – and Gavin’s a lifelong Christian.
She went to school at St. John’s Lutheran Church of Orange, sent her children to St. John’s and still regularly attends.
Gavin accepts my apology and grins. Gavin understands what it’s like to be a tenderfoot.
My feet, pasty white, look I was born to crawl.
• • •
From Gavin’s Grand Canyon blog:
_I woke up in the autumn dark, re-checked my little knapsack of supplies, kissed my husband goodbye, and started down the North Kaibab Trail at 6:30 am. 38 degrees. Cloudy._

_Down, down, down, 14 miles total from the North Rim to Phantom Ranch, inebriated by puddles of canyon-red water, splashing barefoot and leaving lovely exit-prints of the miraculous human foot.”_
• • •
On a Web site where students rank professors on a scale of 1-5, Gavin scores 4.8-4.9 – except for “easiness” where she gets a 3.9.
The weird part? Students call their tough, albeit barefoot, professor a hippie.
Weirder? This so-called hippie used to race motorcycles.
Lesson: Don’t judge a person by their uncover.
But let’s go back to Gavin’s early days. The daughter of a family doctor, Gavin grew up the youngest of seven children.
If you think being the baby of the bunch and finding yourself pregnant at 15 was tough, you would be right.
Like a lot of kids, Gavin was a wild child. But when she became pregnant after only two years of high school, she felt she only had one choice.
Become a full-time Mom.
After visiting Planned Parenthood, the decision didn’t come lightly. Understand, Gavin devoured books, won spelling bees, was her eighth-grade valedictorian.
Now, she was embarking on a journey she had never imagined.
• • •
_“Barefoot?” one lady exclaimed with a big grin, pointing at my feet._
_I replied by pointing back at her feet and saying, “Shoes?”_
_We both laughed. We’re at the bleepin’ Grand Canyon! How could anyone be cranky?_
• • •
In September 1975, Gavin and her equally young boyfriend married. Fortunately, there was love and forgiveness in the air.
The couple’s less-than-thrilled parents attended, even celebrated.
Four months later, Gavin had her first child, a baby boy the couple named Ty.
Named after – what else? – a vintage dirt bike.
“I look at our stupidity and poor choices,” Gavin reflects, “and think, holy cow, I have three amazing kids, five magnificent grandkids and a 37-year marriage.
“You can never screw up bad enough that God can’t help you out.”

If it hadn’t been for their mistake – and the way the young couple handled their wild streak – Gavin allows, “We’d probably be dead by now.”
Perhaps it was coincidence. Perhaps it was something else. But somehow things fell in place.
Gavin’s teenage husband, Steve, had enough money from an accident settlement for a down payment on a modest home.
At an age when most girls think about their junior prom, Gavin borrowed books from the local public library and taught herself to clean, cook, raise a child.
At the same time, Steve started working at his father’s muffler shop. Soon, Gavin found the time to help babysit during Bible study at St. John’s.
Of the congregation, she reports, “They never shunned me, not one bit.”
Two years after Ty was born, the couple added daughter Tina. Their third child followed four years later, baby boy Taylor.
But there were complications.
• • •
_It was barefoot-hiking heaven. The green river frosted with rapids, the sunrise cliffs of contrasting red-gold-and-shadow, dreamy streamside vegetation smells. Sigh._
• • •
Baby Taylor required a tracheotomy and a gastrostomy.
It’s said that you can’t be a care giver if you don’t take care of yourself. And for Gavin that certainly was true. She realized she needed occasional breaks.
With Steve minding the children, Gavin plunged into her husband’s hobby, dirt-bike racing.
She headed to now-closed Saddleback Motocross Park near Irvine Lake. Soon, she started collecting trophies. But it was never about winning.
Paradoxically, it was about finding peace.
Wrapped in the smell of gasoline, the sound of screaming engines and the sting of flying dirt, Gavin lived in the moment, the challenges of being a mother lost in the adrenaline.
But one day she went motorcycle riding and realized it was Mother’s Day. Then she realized something else. Her escape was becoming an obsession.
So, Gavin dialed down the adrenaline a bit and turned to something she’d loved as a child, something pure, simple – running.
Then she returned to one more early love – education.
She started attending Santa Ana College, taking one class a semester, then two. Soon she was a full-time student. University followed. In the spring of 1997, Gavin taught her first class at Concordia.

• • •
_I’m 53 and feeling pretty good. I just hiked across the Grand Canyon, barefoot. More than halfway in the rain._
_OK, I’m nearly cripple. But only when I change from not-moving to moving._
• • •
Six years ago, Gavin took a standup comedy class. The final required performing at a club. With a routine about being pregnant at 16, she invited only her husband and one sister.
But later that same sister goaded Gavin into performing for her parents. They roared. She killed.
Gavin won’t be pregnant again.
But she will be barefoot.
David Whiting’s column appears four days a week; dwhiting@ocregister.com.

**Athletes often have that one thing that fuels their determination to succeed and for women's marathon world record-holder Brigid Kosgei, it is her difficult childhood.**
"When I think back to my humble beginnings and the challenges we went through growing up, I tell myself I cannot go back to that life and it pushes me to do well," the 25-year-old Kenyan athlete told the BBC.
Four years since running her first marathon, which she won, Kosgei is now the fastest woman in history over the 26.2-mile (42.2km) distance.
Last week in the US city of Chicago, she smashed the record set by Briton Paula Radcliffe in London 16 years ago, by a staggering 81 seconds.
Her two hours 14 minutes and four seconds record was six months in the making - with her coach, Eric Kimaiyo, quietly planning the assault.
In September, Kosgei opted not to honour an invitation to represent her country at the World Athletics Championships in Doha.
"We asked for her to be excused because we had planned something special but we didn't speak about it because we didn't want to put her under any pressure," Kimaiyo told the BBC.
But her discipline and dedication is something that has always set her apart.
"You could tell she was a very talented athlete even in training, extremely disciplined and competitive, never liked to be outshone in training," Robert Ngisirei, who coached her while in high school, told the BBC.

# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## Jogging to school
She was one of seven children raised by a single mother in Elgeyo-Marakwet county, a region in the Rift Valley known to produce some of Kenya's top runners.
And like some other Kenyan athletes before her, Kosgei discovered she could run while in primary school, when she had to jog to class in the morning.
"My school was 10km from home and sometimes to avoid getting late I would run. On my way I met athletes who were training and said to myself: 'I can be like them,'" she said.
London 2012: The village at the heart of Kenyan long-distance running
She started competing in middle-distance events at school and though she was never selected to represent her country, her talent was never in doubt.
After raising school fees became a challenge for her mother, Kosgei decided to drop out of school in January 2012 during her final year, given that her studies were now coming second to her track training.
"By the time I was in form three, the arrears were over $1,500 (£1,200). My mother tried to convince me to stay on by saying she would borrow the money but I told her: 'For how long will we keep borrowing?"
texts.2:
# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## Career break to have twins
But now, aged 17, she was able to take her running seriously - something that has repaid her family in spades and pays for all her younger siblings' school fees.
She began training with her boyfriend Mathew Kosgei, who is now her husband. A year later she took a career break after giving birth to twins.
But motherhood did not dent her determination. In 2015 she picked up where she had left off, this time moving to join a training camp not far from her home, run by her coach.
**You may also be interested in:**
*   Born to run: Kenya's top runners  
*   Technology behind record marathon runs
Such camps in Kenya offer athletes an environment where they can focus on training away from the distractions of everyday life.
For female athletes, the decision to stay away from their families, especially children, is often a difficult one but those who do it usually have good family support.
"My husband told me not to worry - he would take care of the children - and that I should just focus on my career and soon the children also got used to seeing me only on the weekends when I'd return home," said Kosgei.
texts.3:
# Kenya's Brigid Kosgei: School dropout, mother of twins and world record-holder
## 'My mother is very happy'
Within months of joining the camp, she ran her first marathon, in November 2015 in Portugal, romping home in first place, beating the competition by more than four minutes.
Her decision to go into marathon running was informed by the very competitive nature of track events.
At her training camp there were more marathon runners and it was easier for her to get training partners.
She now trains with her male teammates to improve her endurance.
"It is very difficult training with them because they are very fast but when I want to give up, I tell myself: 'No, keep moving.'"
Her season is over but she is ranked the top female marathon runner of 2019. Next year her focus will turn to the biggest sports event of all - the Olympic Games.
She is now heading back to her home village to visit her mum, for whom she has bought land and a house with her previous winnings, and will spend time with her husband and children.
"My mother is waiting for me to get back home and she was very happy when I broke the record," she said.

Sometimes a mistake turns into the best decision you ever made.
I meet Thea Gavin, grandmother of five, and can’t help staring at her feet.
Yes, feet.
Gavin, professor at Concordia University Irvine and recipient of two master’s degrees, isn’t wearing shoes. Or socks.
Since Gavin’s a barefoot runner, her lack of footwear is expected. We head off on a run, with me wearing shoes. As we run and chat, Gavin’s life story starts to unfold, and I realize her story is about far more than running barefoot.
It’s about trust, love and faith.
It’s also about a high school dropout who had her first child at 16.
Yes, _those_ were mistakes.
But her recent rim-to-rim Grand Canyon hike – barefoot – was intentional.
• • •
Ever the professor, Gavin agrees to share if I promise to make this column a teachable moment – and funny.
Funny’s hard and the professor’s assignment scares the bejeebers out of me. But what scares me more is knowing that at some time during our run, according to my own weird code, I must remove my shoes and run barefoot.
Why run shoeless? I call it reporting. My wife calls it nuts.
Gavin, 53, glides along a rocky trail as if she were born to run.
For a few hundred yards, I run on soft dirt and feel like Huck Finn. Then I hit a rough patch. Ouch. Then pebbles. Ouch, ouch. Then rocks…
I blurt something one shouldn’t, especially around a Christian – and Gavin’s a lifelong Christian.
She went to school at St. John’s Lutheran Church of Orange, sent her children to St. John’s and still regularly attends.
Gavin accepts my apology and grins. Gavin understands what it’s like to be a tenderfoot.
My feet, pasty white, look I was born to crawl.
• • •
From Gavin’s Grand Canyon blog:
_I woke up in the autumn dark, re-checked my little knapsack of supplies, kissed my husband goodbye, and started down the North Kaibab Trail at 6:30 am. 38 degrees. Cloudy._
texts.1:
_Down, down, down, 14 miles total from the North Rim to Phantom Ranch, inebriated by puddles of canyon-red water, splashing barefoot and leaving lovely exit-prints of the miraculous human foot.”_
• • •
On a Web site where students rank professors on a scale of 1-5, Gavin scores 4.8-4.9 – except for “easiness” where she gets a 3.9.
The weird part? Students call their tough, albeit barefoot, professor a hippie.
Weirder? This so-called hippie used to race motorcycles.
Lesson: Don’t judge a person by their uncover.
But let’s go back to Gavin’s early days. The daughter of a family doctor, Gavin grew up the youngest of seven children.
If you think being the baby of the bunch and finding yourself pregnant at 15 was tough, you would be right.
Like a lot of kids, Gavin was a wild child. But when she became pregnant after only two years of high school, she felt she only had one choice.
Become a full-time Mom.
After visiting Planned Parenthood, the decision didn’t come lightly. Understand, Gavin devoured books, won spelling bees, was her eighth-grade valedictorian.
Now, she was embarking on a journey she had never imagined.
• • •
_“Barefoot?” one lady exclaimed with a big grin, pointing at my feet._
_I replied by pointing back at her feet and saying, “Shoes?”_
_We both laughed. We’re at the bleepin’ Grand Canyon! How could anyone be cranky?_
• • •
In September 1975, Gavin and her equally young boyfriend married. Fortunately, there was love and forgiveness in the air.
The couple’s less-than-thrilled parents attended, even celebrated.
Four months later, Gavin had her first child, a baby boy the couple named Ty.
Named after – what else? – a vintage dirt bike.
“I look at our stupidity and poor choices,” Gavin reflects, “and think, holy cow, I have three amazing kids, five magnificent grandkids and a 37-year marriage.
“You can never screw up bad enough that God can’t help you out.”
texts.2:
If it hadn’t been for their mistake – and the way the young couple handled their wild streak – Gavin allows, “We’d probably be dead by now.”
Perhaps it was coincidence. Perhaps it was something else. But somehow things fell in place.
Gavin’s teenage husband, Steve, had enough money from an accident settlement for a down payment on a modest home.
At an age when most girls think about their junior prom, Gavin borrowed books from the local public library and taught herself to clean, cook, raise a child.
At the same time, Steve started working at his father’s muffler shop. Soon, Gavin found the time to help babysit during Bible study at St. John’s.
Of the congregation, she reports, “They never shunned me, not one bit.”
Two years after Ty was born, the couple added daughter Tina. Their third child followed four years later, baby boy Taylor.
But there were complications.
• • •
_It was barefoot-hiking heaven. The green river frosted with rapids, the sunrise cliffs of contrasting red-gold-and-shadow, dreamy streamside vegetation smells. Sigh._
• • •
Baby Taylor required a tracheotomy and a gastrostomy.
It’s said that you can’t be a care giver if you don’t take care of yourself. And for Gavin that certainly was true. She realized she needed occasional breaks.
With Steve minding the children, Gavin plunged into her husband’s hobby, dirt-bike racing.
She headed to now-closed Saddleback Motocross Park near Irvine Lake. Soon, she started collecting trophies. But it was never about winning.
Paradoxically, it was about finding peace.
Wrapped in the smell of gasoline, the sound of screaming engines and the sting of flying dirt, Gavin lived in the moment, the challenges of being a mother lost in the adrenaline.
But one day she went motorcycle riding and realized it was Mother’s Day. Then she realized something else. Her escape was becoming an obsession.
So, Gavin dialed down the adrenaline a bit and turned to something she’d loved as a child, something pure, simple – running.
Then she returned to one more early love – education.
She started attending Santa Ana College, taking one class a semester, then two. Soon she was a full-time student. University followed. In the spring of 1997, Gavin taught her first class at Concordia.
texts.3:
• • •
_I’m 53 and feeling pretty good. I just hiked across the Grand Canyon, barefoot. More than halfway in the rain._
_OK, I’m nearly cripple. But only when I change from not-moving to moving._
• • •
Six years ago, Gavin took a standup comedy class. The final required performing at a club. With a routine about being pregnant at 16, she invited only her husband and one sister.
But later that same sister goaded Gavin into performing for her parents. They roared. She killed.
Gavin won’t be pregnant again.
But she will be barefoot.

Anjuman  Ara  received  a  scholarship  to attend  Chitoshi  High  School.  She  was  
thirteen  years  old, with  nine  brothers  and  sisters.  Her  father  finished  primary  
school  and  is  a  rice  farmer;  her  mother  is  illiterate.  Her  friend,  Majeda,  was  
already  married  and  expecting  a  baby.  In  the  poor  Sharasti  upazila,  a  rural  
region  in  the  Comilla  district  of Bangladesh,  Majeda  was  the  rule rather  than  
the  exception.  She,  unlike  her  brothers,  was  an  economic  burden  to  her  fam-  
ily;  at fourteen,  she  was  married  and  shipped to  her  in-laws.  
Given  parental  attitudes  about  daughters,  it  is  not  surprising  that  the  1981  
census  reported  that  the  average  age  of marriage  was  16.8  years  for  females  
but  23.9  years  for  males  and  that  only  4.7  percent  of females  but  10.6  percent  
of males  had  some  secondary  schooling.  This  information  is even  less  surpris-  
ing  in  a  country  where  the  main  reason  for  not  sending  children  to  school  is  
poverty,  where  fewer  than  2  percent  of secondary  schools  are  operated  by  the  
government,  and where  parents  must  bear the  cost  not  only  of tuition  but  also  
of  transportation,  books,  supplies,  uniforms,  admission  fees,  examination  
fees,  the  poor  fund,  and  snacks.  No  wonder  Majeda's  family  was  anxious  to  
ship  her  off to  in-laws  so  she  could  fulfill  her  role  as  obedient  wife  and  fertile

mother.  Majeda  can  be  expected  to  bear  seven  children,  contributing  to  an  
alarming  3  percent  annual  rate of population  growth  in  the  country.
